proposals.name: Kadovar — The Funeral Republic
proposals.entry:
Common Name: Kadovar
Government: The Funeral Republic
People: Kadovarians
Capital: Veyr Kadovar
Status: Active belligerent in the War of 100 Kingdoms
Major Exports: Iron, copper, mineral salts, surgical instruments, glass, embalming compounds, prosthetics, preserved flowers, battlefield recovery services

Kadovar died 312 years ago.

The country survived.

The Pale Weather

Kadovar was once a small mountain kingdom of black forests, mineral-rich valleys and fortified industrial towns.

During an old border war, an enemy alchemical corps devised a weapon intended to kill Kadovar's population without destroying the mines, roads and factories they intended to capture.

Official military documents called it P-17 Atmospheric Mortality Compound.

History remembers it as the Pale Weather.

Shells burst along Kadovar's western mountains and released a heavy pearl-colored vapor. The mountains trapped it. The gas poured through the valleys, into villages and eventually through the streets of Veyr Kadovar.

Animals died. Crops withered. Soldiers collapsed in their trenches.

Within eleven days, almost the entire population of Kadovar was dead.

The invading army waited for the gas to clear.

Then Kadovar got back up.

The Second Morning

The Pale Weather did not restore life.

Kadovarian hearts remained still. Their blood no longer circulated normally. Their bodies were cold and they no longer needed to breathe except to speak.

Yet memory, personality and consciousness remained.

The first days were chaos. Families searched for one another. Fires burned unattended. Corpses woke beneath collapsed buildings. Surgeons who were themselves dead attempted to understand patients who were equally dead.

Then practical matters asserted themselves. Fires needed extinguishing. Food stores needed securing, even if nobody was quite certain who still needed food. The border remained undefended. Someone needed to bury the invading soldiers. And the government still existed.

Kadovar resumed operations.

The anniversary is commemorated as the Second Morning.

The Funeral Republic

The old monarchy eventually collapsed, although Kadovar itself did not.

Its successor became known as the Funeral Republic.

Kadovarian law gradually abandoned the idea that a person's body constituted their legal identity. Citizenship instead rests upon continuity of identity: memory, personality and recognized existence.

This became necessary because Kadovarian medicine discovered something remarkable.

Dead Kadovarian tissue could be repaired. And replaced.

A Nation of Repairs

The Pale Weather left something behind in Kadovarian flesh. Decay slowed enormously, and dead tissue could accept transplanted tissue with astonishing success.

A ruined hand could be replaced. A shattered leg could be exchanged. Skin could be patched. Bones could be pinned, wired or substituted.

Kadovar developed mortuary surgery, eventually becoming the greatest center of anatomical reconstruction in the known kingdoms.

Hospitals maintain carefully catalogued Common Anatomical Reserves, supplied by Kadovarians whose bodies can no longer support their identities.

Unauthorized harvesting is one of Kadovar's most serious crimes.

A citizen's body may change considerably over the centuries. Their citizenship does not.

A Dwindling Country

There is one terrible fact beneath Kadovar's apparent immortality.

There are no new Kadovarians.

The Pale Weather happened once.

Every Kadovarian alive today is one of the people who died 312 years ago.

Bodies can be repaired. Parts can be replaced. But when enough of a Kadovarian is destroyed that their identity is truly lost, that person is gone. Forever.

Kadovar therefore possesses a population that can endure for centuries but can only become smaller.

Every permanent death is a measurable reduction in the nation.

What Kadovar Sells

The mountains that inspired Kadovar's destruction remain rich in iron, copper, zinc and strange pale mineral salts.

Kadovarian glass is famous. Its surgical instruments are among the finest in the 100 Kingdoms. Its chemists produce preservatives, dyes, medicines and embalming compounds. Its surgeons manufacture sophisticated prosthetics and replacement structures intended for both living and dead patients.

Kadovar also exports one surprisingly beautiful commodity: dead flowers.

Flowers exposed to carefully diluted derivatives of Pale Weather cease living but retain their shape and color for decades.

Kadovarian pale roses are expensive, fashionable and considered either romantic or deeply inappropriate depending upon the kingdom.

The War of 100 Kingdoms

Kadovar attempted to remain outside the present war.

It had already experienced extermination once.

For years Kadovarian companies instead sold medical services, battlefield retrieval and specialized engineering to foreign armies.

Then a neighboring belligerent attempted to annex Kadovarian territory.

Its legal justification was extraordinary: Dead people could not possess sovereign land.

Kadovar considered the argument answered when its army crossed the border.

It has been at war ever since.

The Kadovarian Army

Kadovarian soldiers are difficult to permanently kill. They are not indestructible.

A bullet may incapacitate one. Artillery can tear one apart. Fire remains particularly feared because it destroys tissue rather than merely damaging it.

After every battle, Retrieval Companies search the field.

Kadovarian soldiers carry identification markers in several locations on their bodies. Recovered remains are sorted, catalogued and returned to mortuary hospitals.

Sometimes a soldier returns on a stretcher. Sometimes in a coffin. Sometimes in several numbered canvas bags.

Whatever can be reconstructed is reconstructed. What cannot be recovered may be replaced from the Common Anatomical Reserve.

Old Kadovarian soldiers therefore become increasingly patched as a war continues. Their stitches are campaign scars.

Nobody Left Behind

Other armies admire Kadovar's famous refusal to abandon its casualties.

They often misunderstand it as military honor.

It is more desperate than that.

Kadovar cannot recruit another generation. It cannot replace a permanently destroyed soldier.

Every missing body on a battlefield represents a citizen who might still be recoverable.

So Retrieval Companies sometimes enter fields while the guns are still firing.

Nobody gets left behind.

Not because Kadovar has endless soldiers.

Because it has exactly as many as it will ever have.

Kadovar Today

Kadovar remains a beautiful, unsettling country of steep roofs, dark forests, mineral towns, glass conservatories and pale gardens that never wilt.

Undertakers perform much of the work physicians perform elsewhere. Hospitals have enormous basements. Tailors understand where surgeons prefer garments to open.

Citizens argue about elections, money, art, romance, factory wages and the war. They drink despite having little biological need to do so. They marry. They feud. They travel. They make plans for futures measured in centuries.

Kadovar is not an evil country. Nor has dying made its people particularly virtuous.

It has corrupt politicians, criminals, profiteers, patriots, cowards, artists, fanatics and decent people trying to get through another day.

Kadovar died 312 years ago.

It regards this primarily as a historical inconvenience.
